answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any disruption to delivery cadence is high-risk right now, which rules out switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor (c2 explicitly documents SLA misses in 3 of 4 quarters and warns against sole-sourcing them for a critical line). Adding a second source addresses a different problem (supply constraint) and doesn't resolve the 14-day contract expiry or the cost mandate. Deferring is not viable because this is not the non-critical, has-slack situation described in c5 — the contract expires in 14 days and the line has no buffer, so month-to-month drift is riskier here. Renewing incumbent as-is doesn't address the 18% spend cut mandate. Negotiating terms with the incumbent (c4) directly targets margin recovery via benchmarking while preserving the stable integration and delivery continuity documented in c1, minimizing TCO without introducing new delivery risk. I verify c4 to confirm the negotiation outcome was durable and not a one-off, and c2 to confirm the severity/frequency of the low-cost vendor's SLA failures before ruling out switching. This is a single-cycle negotiation with the existing supplier, not a novel untested arrangement, so I scope it as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout, and flag downstream delivery-risk exposure explicitly since the 94% utilization leaves no margin for error if the negotiation strains the relationship.
